label: Agents
title: Agents
subtitle: An agent is an AI assistant with a specific role, set of tools, and instructions that tell it how to behave. InnoviumAI lets you run multiple agents — each one is good at something different, and they can hand work off to each other. You choose which agent to talk to, and it handles the task using whatever tools and knowledge it has been given.

subsections.title: What is an Agent?
subsections.description: Think of an agent as a specialist on your team. You describe what it should focus on, give it access to the tools it needs (like web search, code execution, or file access), and write a brief set of instructions that shape how it responds. There are three types. A Simple Agent handles a single task end-to-end — it reasons through the problem and uses its tools until it has an answer. A PI Agent (Principal Investigator) is designed to coordinate longer, multi-phase work: it breaks a big task into a series of milestones, then manages execution phase by phase. An MCP Agent connects to an external service and acts as a bridge between your conversation and that service. Most users start with Simple Agents; PI Agents become useful once you are running projects that span several distinct stages.
subsections.mediaCaption: The three agent types — Simple, PI, and MCP — as they appear when creating a new agent

subsections.title: Choosing an Execution Backend
subsections.description: When you create a custom agent, you can pick the engine that runs it. The default is InnoviumAI's own native engine — it reasons step by step, calls its tools, and works with any model provider. You can instead run an agent on the Claude Agent SDK, which uses Anthropic's native tool-calling for stronger coding and file-editing work (it requires a Claude model). The backend is just how the agent thinks under the hood — the role, tools, and instructions you give it stay the same either way. If you are unsure, leave it on the InnoviumAI native engine; you can always create another agent on the Claude SDK backend and compare. The built-in Code Agent already runs on the Claude SDK, so picking that backend for a custom agent gives you a Code-Agent-style assistant with your own prompt and tools.
subsections.mediaCaption: The Execution Backend selector in the agent creation form — InnoviumAI (native) or Claude Agent SDK

subsections.title: Code Agent Authentication — "Use my subscription"
subsections.description: Agents that run on the Claude Agent SDK (the built-in Code Agent, and any custom agent you put on that backend) need access to Claude. By default they use the shared dashboard — your organisation's managed Claude access — so you don't have to set anything up. If you have Claude installed on your own machine and are signed in to it, you can switch the agent to "Use my subscription" instead, which routes its requests through your local Claude using your own Claude account. The toggle only becomes available when both conditions are met: a local Claude is installed AND you are logged in to it (the `claude` command-line tool is signed in). If Claude is installed but you have not signed in, the app shows "Local Claude found, but not logged in" and the toggle stays disabled until you log in. If Claude is not installed at all, the toggle is disabled. When you choose "Use my subscription", the agent's requests go through your local Claude and count against your own usage and billing rather than the shared dashboard; leave it off to keep using the managed dashboard access, which is the right choice for most users.
subsections.mediaCaption: The "Use my subscription" authentication toggle in the Code Agent settings, disabled with the "Local Claude found, but not logged in" notice

subsections.title: The Agent Panel
subsections.description: The left sidebar lists every enabled agent. Click an agent's name or avatar to select it — the chat area will now send your messages to that agent. Each entry shows the agent's name and a short description so you can tell them apart at a glance. A settings icon appears when you hover over an agent's row; clicking it opens that agent's configuration without leaving the current project. If you do not see an agent you expect, it may be disabled — check Settings > Agents to enable it.
subsections.mediaCaption: The agent list in the left sidebar, showing agent avatars, names, and the hover settings icon

subsections.title: Built-in Tools
subsections.description: Some model providers ship their own server-side tools that run inside the model itself rather than on your machine — for example web search, which can also read the pages it finds, and OpenAI's code interpreter. An agent's settings show a Built-in Tools section that lists the tools compatible with the agent's currently selected model, each with its own on/off switch. Each toggle is saved with the agent and applies to every message it sends. Which tools appear depends on the model: web search runs on both OpenAI and Anthropic models while the others are OpenAI-only, so if the agent is set to a model whose provider offers none, the section simply notes that no built-in tools are available for the current model — switch the agent to a model that supports them and they reappear. Built-in tools are independent of the regular tools you assign in the Tools section — you can use either, both, or neither.
subsections.mediaCaption: The Built-in Tools toggles in agent settings, shown for an agent using an OpenAI model

subsections.title: Sharing an Agent with Your Profile or Organisation
subsections.description: An agent you have tuned does not have to stay on your machine. Open Settings > Agents and click the share icon on the agent's row. The icon only appears when there is something worth sending — an agent you created, or a built-in one you have changed; a pristine built-in shows no share icon, because everyone already has it. The dialog is titled "Share Agent:" followed by the agent's name, and it opens on "Share with User". That route hands the agent straight to one person in your profile: search for them by name or email, and the agent is created on their side once they accept it. The other two routes go through review. "Share with Profile" sends the agent to the people who manage your profile, so it can become a default for everyone in it. "Share with Organization" aims it at the organisation-wide catalog, where an administrator decides instead of your profile manager; it is offered only for an agent you built from scratch, not for one you derived from a built-in. The button at the bottom of the dialog names what will actually happen: it reads Publish when you are submitting a whole agent of your own, and Propose when you are offering your changes to an agent that came from the catalog. Once you confirm, the app acknowledges that the agent has been sent, and nobody else in your profile sees it until it is approved. The two refusals below belong to Publish, because only a published agent takes a name in the catalog. If the catalog already holds another agent under that name the submission is refused, and the message usually names a variation that is free — for example that "Engineering Lead (2)" is available — so rename the agent as suggested and submit it again. If you are publishing something already sitting in the queue, the message says so instead of filing a second copy. A Propose is checked neither way: it is a request about an agent the catalog already holds, so send it once and wait, because proposing the same change again files a second request alongside the first.
subsections.mediaCaption: The Share Agent dialog with the Share with Profile route selected and the Publish button ready

subsections.title: How a Submission Is Reviewed
subsections.description: A submission does not go live on its own. It lands under Proposals in the dashboard, in front of whoever can decide on it: a manager of your profile for a profile submission, an organisation administrator for an organisation-wide one. Each entry carries your name and when you sent it — and, for an agent you published in full, the profile it came from — so a reviewer can tell submissions apart. The reviewer clicks Review to read the agent itself rather than just its name and description. When your submission changes something that already exists, the review opens on a line-by-line diff of what you altered, with a Diff/Full toggle for switching between just your changes and the whole configuration. The reviewer then chooses Approve or Reject. On an agent you published in full they can also leave a note explaining the decision; a proposed change is approved or rejected without one. That decision and any note live in the dashboard for now; the app does not yet tell you either way, so ask a manager of your profile where a submission stands. An approved agent reaches everyone in the profile at their next sync. A rejected one leaves your own copy untouched, so the agent is still yours to work on in Settings > Agents. An agent you published in full keeps its name when you send it again: your fixed version replaces the rejected submission rather than filing a second one, so hold on to the name while you work on it. A rejected proposal holds no name for you, so once you have fixed it, simply propose the change again.
subsections.mediaCaption: The Proposals page in the dashboard with a submission open on its line-by-line diff, the Diff and Full toggles above it

subsections.title: Exporting an Agent File
subsections.description: Export an agent when you want to keep a copy of its configuration outside the app. Open Settings > Agents, find the agent in the list, and click the download icon on its row — the app downloads an `<agent-id>.agent.zip` file to wherever your browser saves downloads. The file holds the agent's prompt, tools, and skills. Both your custom agents and the built-in system agents can be exported. To hand an agent to someone else, use the share icon on the same row.
subsections.mediaCaption: The Agents settings panel with the per-agent download icon
